Where is Des Moines and how is the city laid out?

Des Moines is the capital of Iowa and the seat of Polk County, built where the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers meet. The city covers about 90 square miles, and the part south of County Line Road reaches into Warren County.

Most house sellers deal with a few distinct areas. Downtown and the East Village sit near the State Capitol on the east side of the Des Moines River. South of Grand is the older neighborhood around Salisbury House. Around the city limits are the suburbs of West Des Moines, Urbandale, Ankeny, Altoona, Clive, Johnston and Windsor Heights, which compete with city houses for the same buyers.

The 2020 census counted 214,133 people in the city and 709,466 in the metro area, which makes Des Moines the largest city in the state by a wide margin. The median age in the city is 34.8.

What does Des Moines history mean for an older house?

Des Moines began as Fort Des Moines in 1843 and became the state capital in 1857, so many of its older streets date to the railroad and coal era. Captain James Allen supervised construction of the fort in May 1843, and the army left in 1846.

A flood destroyed much of the town in May 1851, and the city was incorporated on September 22, 1851. The capital moved here from Iowa City in 1857, when the name was shortened from Fort Des Moines. A rail link finished in 1866 sped up growth, and coal mining ran from the 1860s until the supply was largely used up by 1908. By 1880 Des Moines was the largest city in Iowa.

That timeline explains why one block can hold houses from very different decades. Buyers of older houses usually ask for inspections of the plumbing, wiring and basement. Sellers who would rather not pay for repairs before listing can sell the house as it stands.

Insurance and finance are the core of the Des Moines economy, and the city is nicknamed the Hartford of the West. Principal Financial Group and Wellmark Blue Cross Blue Shield are headquartered here, and Iowa's 1 percent insurance premium tax is cited as one reason insurers locate in the state.

What flood history should a Des Moines seller know?

Des Moines has flooded repeatedly, and buyers and lenders ask about it. The 1851 flood wiped out much of the early town. During the Great Flood of 1993 the Des Moines Water Works was submerged on July 11, and about 250,000 people lost running water for 12 days and drinking water for 20 days.

Floods returned in June 2008, when a levee breached. The Birdland neighborhood on the north side, along the Des Moines River, flooded in both 1993 and 2008. It later got a rebuilt levee that cost $11 million, runs wider in many places and stands roughly 2 to 4 feet taller than the old one. Officials said tree growth had weakened the earlier levee and contributed to the 2008 failure, and they also said the new one does not remove flood risk.

  • Ask your insurance agent whether the parcel sits in a mapped flood zone before you set a closing date.
  • Keep any repair receipts and claim paperwork from past water damage. Buyers ask for them.
  • If the house has a damp basement, say so up front. A cash buyer prices the condition in and does not need a repair list from you.

How do schools, roads and transit affect Des Moines sellers?

Most of the city belongs to the Des Moines Independent Community School District, the largest in Iowa. The district listed 65 schools and 33,739 students in 2022-23, with East, Hoover, Lincoln, North and Roosevelt high schools plus an online campus. Small parts of Pleasant Hill and Windsor Heights fall in the district too.

Interstate 235 runs through the city, while I-35 and I-80 run together on the north side. Des Moines International Airport sits on Fleur Drive in the south. DART provides bus service with local, commuter and express routes, and there is no passenger rail in the city. The nearest Amtrak station is in Osceola, about 40 miles south.

Colleges add another buyer and renter group. Drake University, Grand View University and Mercy College of Health Sciences all have main campuses here, along with Des Moines University and a Des Moines Area Community College presence.

What local rules apply to rentals and neglected houses in Des Moines?

A Des Moines owner who rents out a house needs a rental certificate from the city. The Neighborhood Services Inspection Division inspects rentals and enforces the requirement when a house is rented without one.

The city's application form says the owner's name must match the Polk County Assessor's records and that an owner living outside Polk County and its bordering counties must name a local management agent who is an adult. An owner who does not return the completed form within 10 days commits a municipal infraction, and a $26 research fee applies if the form comes back late.

The same division handles junk and debris, junk vehicles, illegal dumping, noise, graffiti and condemned buildings. It is located at 602 Robert D. Ray Drive, 2nd floor. A vacant or inherited house that attracts complaints can pick up violations quickly.

  • Gather the rental certificate if the house has been a rental.
  • Clear open code complaints, or tell a buyer about them in writing.
  • Confirm the owner name on the deed matches the assessor record.

When are Polk County property taxes due, and what happens at a sale?

Polk County property tax is due in two halves, September 1 and March 1, and it becomes delinquent after September 30 and March 31. If the last day lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day. Late interest is 1.5 percent per month, with a $1 minimum.

The Polk County Treasurer's office can be reached at 515-286-3060. Payments must be postmarked by the due date to count as on time, and online payment is available at Iowa Tax and Tags. Unpaid taxes can be sold at the county tax sale, which uses online bidding. In 2024 the sale was June 17, and owners could pay before 5:00 p.m. on June 14 to keep their parcel off it.

At a sale, taxes are normally prorated. The buyer receives a credit for the seller's share, or the seller pays the treasurer directly at closing. Iowa taxes run a year behind, so the September and March bills cover July 1 through June 30 of the prior year. Check your settlement statement.

Iowa also charges a transfer tax of eighty cents per $500 of value above the first $500, and a declaration of value must go in with the recorded deed (Iowa Code 428A.1).

How does a cash sale work for a Des Moines house?

In a cash sale the buyer does not need a mortgage, so there is no lender appraisal and no loan approval to wait on. That can matter for houses with open permits, old systems or deferred repairs, which lenders sometimes will not approve.

  • You receive a written offer that you can accept or turn down.
  • If you accept, a title company handles the paperwork and the property taxes are settled at closing.
  • You pick the closing date within what the title work allows.

If the house is an inherited Des Moines property, a rental with tenants, or a home behind on payments, tell us up front. Those situations change the paperwork, not the basic steps.

Des Moines is the seat of Polk County, and the part of the city south of County Line Road extends into Warren County. Property tax for most Des Moines houses is billed by the Polk County Treasurer.

Yes. The city requires a rental certificate and its Neighborhood Services Inspection Division enforces it. The owner of record must return the application within 10 days or face a municipal infraction.

When are Polk County property taxes delinquent?

The first half is delinquent after September 30 and the second half after March 31. Interest then runs at 1.5 percent per month with a $1 minimum.

Do Des Moines houses flood?

Some do. Low areas near the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers flooded in 1851, 1993 and 2008, and the Birdland neighborhood on the north side has been rebuilt behind a new levee. Ask your insurer about the parcel.

Can I sell a Des Moines house with code violations?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house as it stands, and any violations or liens are settled through the title company at closing or handled as the contract states.

Where is Cedar Rapids and how is the city divided?

Cedar Rapids is the county seat of Linn County, about 20 miles north of Iowa City and 128 miles northeast of Des Moines. It is the second most populous city in Iowa, with 137,710 residents in the 2020 census and a Census Bureau estimate of 137,935 for 2025.

The Cedar River splits the city into east and west sides, and 1st Avenue (U.S. Route 151 Business) splits it north from south. That makes four address quadrants. The city uses 14 ZIP codes, with downtown and Mays Island in 52401, so the first thing to confirm in any listing or offer is the exact quadrant and ZIP.

The city covers about 76 square miles at an elevation of 810 feet.

What is the history of Cedar Rapids?

Osgood Shepherd built the first cabin in 1837 or 1838, and the town was platted in 1841 as Rapids City. It was incorporated as Cedar Rapids on January 15, 1849, with fewer than 400 people.

Czech immigrants made up a large part of the early population: in 1856 about a quarter of roughly 1,600 residents were Czech. The first locomotive arrived on June 15, 1859. Sinclair meatpacking started in 1871 and the Quaker Oats mill was built in 1873. The county seat moved from Marion to Cedar Rapids in 1919.

Population passed 110,000 by 1970 and has grown slowly since, reaching 126,326 in 2010.

How did flooding and the 2020 derecho affect Cedar Rapids housing?

Cedar Rapids has two kinds of recent storm history that a seller needs to understand, river flooding and wind. Both left marks on the housing stock and on buyers' questions.

  • June 2008 flood: the Cedar River crested at a record 31.12 feet on June 13, against a previous record of 20 feet. Some 1,126 city blocks flooded, 7,749 properties were evacuated, including 5,900 homes, and at least 1,300 properties had to be demolished.
  • September 2016 flood: the river reached 22 feet on September 27, the second highest crest on record, with flood stage at 12 feet. More than 5,000 homes were affected. The city approved a $625 million, 20-year levee plan in 2015.
  • August 10, 2020 derecho: sustained winds of 60 to 80 mph and gusts of 110 mph or more hit the city. About 95 percent of Cedar Rapids lost power and 20 schools were damaged.

If a house sits in an area that took water or wind damage, expect a conventional buyer's inspection to look hard at the basement, roof and electrical system. A cash purchase can skip that repair negotiation.

Cedar Rapids requires rental housing to hold a Certificate of Compliance before it can be legally occupied. The city issues it once the property meets the Housing Code and registration and inspection charges are paid.

Annual registration fees on the city's rental housing page are $50 for a single-family unit or condominium, $60 for a duplex, and $42 plus $13 per unit for a multi-family structure. A separate inspection fee schedule took effect July 1, 2023.

A landlord who is tired of managing a rental house can sell it with tenants in place or after they move out. Ask the buyer whether the registration will transfer or needs to be filed again.

What does Iowa require at a Cedar Rapids closing?

Every Iowa deed that moves through the Linn County Recorder carries a declaration of value, and most also carry a groundwater hazard statement. Iowa Code 558.69 sets out what the seller must report.

  • Wells, with approximate location and whether they meet state rules.
  • Private burial sites, underground storage tanks and known hazardous waste.
  • Solid waste disposal sites identified by the Department of Natural Resources.
  • Private sewage disposal systems, and whether they were inspected or are exempt at transfer.

At least one seller or the seller's agent signs it, and the buyer receives a copy. The owner is responsible for the accuracy of the answers. After the 2008 flood, owners of older properties should check records carefully for any tank or well that was removed, capped or replaced.

Where is Davenport, Iowa, and what is the Quad Cities?

Davenport is the county seat of Scott County and sits on the Mississippi River at the eastern edge of Iowa. It is one of the five Quad Cities, together with Bettendorf in Iowa and Rock Island, Moline and East Moline in Illinois.

The city covers about 66 square miles at an elevation of 660 feet. The river runs east to west here, and the ground slopes up to the north. The 2020 census counted 101,724 residents, which makes Davenport the third most populous city in Iowa after Des Moines and Cedar Rapids. The metro area had 381,801 people.

What is the history of Davenport?

Antoine Le Claire settled Davenport on May 14, 1836, and named it for George Davenport. The city was incorporated on January 25, 1839. The 1832 Black Hawk Purchase, covering about 6 million acres for $640,000, had opened the land to settlement.

The first railroad bridge across the Mississippi opened in 1856 and linked Davenport to Rock Island, Illinois. Abraham Lincoln was the railroad's lead defense lawyer in the litigation that followed a steamboat collision that May. Past industries here included locomotive manufacturing, meatpacking and a Caterpillar loader plant that later closed.

The population has hovered around 100,000 for about four decades, and the 2024 estimate of 100,938 sits right on that line. A flat population means sellers here are not counting on a surge of newcomers, so condition and price carry the sale.

How serious is flooding in Davenport?

Davenport has no permanent flood wall or levee, which makes it the largest city on the Mississippi River without one. The older flood wall dates from 1919.

  • The city requires new construction in the floodplain to be elevated or protected by walls.
  • The 1993 Great Flood crested at 22.63 feet on July 9, nearly 8 feet above flood stage.
  • The river flooded again in 2019 and 2023, while higher walls protected downtown Rock Island and Bettendorf in 2019.
  • Credit Island stayed closed for 5.5 months after the 2008 flooding.

Anyone selling a riverside house should expect buyers to ask whether the lot is in a floodplain and whether the house has ever taken water. A cash buyer will ask the same questions but can price the answer in directly.

It runs four public high schools (Central, West, Mid City and North), six intermediate schools and 23 elementary schools. Assumption is the private high school.

Higher education includes St. Ambrose University, founded in 1882, Palmer College of Chiropractic, Kaplan University and Hamilton Technical College. Much of the housing stock here is old, because the city grew early. It was founded in 1854, laid out that winter, and incorporated on January 16, 1857. An elevated steam railway opened in 1891 and closed within about ten years, which tells you how fast the city was building in that era.

Several neighborhoods carry that age directly:

  • Rose Hill has large, century-old houses.
  • The Heights has estates built from the 1890s to the 1940s, including Prairie School homes.
  • Morningside began as a late-19th-century streetcar suburb on hilly ground.
  • Indian Hills was built between the 1960s and the 1980s.

A house from that era can carry original plumbing, plaster walls or an older foundation, and those are the items a buyer's inspector tends to flag. Owners who would rather not pay for those repairs sometimes look at an as-is sale.

  • Foundation and basement moisture show up in spring, when snowmelt and rain arrive together.

It can, mostly for homes near the Missouri River and the Big Sioux River. The Missouri River stage at Sioux City reached 35.25 feet on July 21, 2011, more than four feet above the previous high set in 1984, according to National Weather Service flood records.

That 2011 event also closed Interstate 29 for about two months, and the 2019 Midwest floods closed a long stretch of I-29 south of here, from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Council Bluffs. Riverside, one of the city's flat neighborhoods, lies on the Big Sioux floodplain.

Bomgaars, Mercy Medical Center, UnityPoint Health St. Luke's, Hy-Vee, the 185th Air Refueling Wing and the City of Sioux City are also major employers.

The Sioux City Community School District runs three public high schools (West, North and East), three middle schools and 19 elementary schools. Higher education includes Briar Cliff University, Morningside University, Western Iowa Tech Community College and St. Luke's College of Nursing.

Interstate 29 runs through the city and Interstate 129 serves as a bypass, with U.S. Route 20 also passing through. Sioux Gateway Airport is about six miles south, Sioux City Transit runs local bus lines and Jefferson Lines provides intercity service. Sioux City Inspection Services handles building permits, rental housing permits and property maintenance complaints, and its office is at 405 6th Street. Work done without a permit is investigated, so unpermitted finished basements, decks or rewiring can surface during a sale.

The city's enforcement tools include municipal infraction citations of $100 to $500 for each initial violation, nuisance notices that let the city clean up a lot and bill the owner, and demolition notices for unsafe buildings. Woodbury County property tax is paid in two halves: the first is due September 1 and goes delinquent October 1, and the second is due March 1 and goes delinquent April 1. Late taxes accrue interest at 1.5 percent per month. The Treasurer's office is at 822 Douglas Street, Room 102, in Sioux City.

Where is Johnston and what are its boundaries?

Johnston is a city in Polk County on the northwest side of the Des Moines metro area. Interstate 80 forms its southern border, the Des Moines River marks the east, and the western limits run to about a half mile east of Iowa Highway 141.

The city covers roughly 20.9 square miles by one count, and part of Saylorville Reservoir lies inside it. Beaver Creek runs south through town before turning east toward the river. One regional guide places Johnston about 10.5 miles from downtown Des Moines.

The 2020 census counted 24,064 residents, up from 8,649 in 2000, and the 2025 estimate is 25,065. The city has 9,194 households and a median age of 37.0, and it ranks 24th in Iowa by population.

How did Johnston begin?

Johnston started in 1905 as Johnston Station, a stop on the Des Moines and Central Iowa Railway between Des Moines and Perry. It was named for railway freight supervisor John F. Johnston. Passenger service ended in 1949.

Voters approved incorporation on June 23, 1969. In April 1970 Johnston and Urbandale reached an agreement that let Johnston annex the Johnston Station area. The city runs on a mayor-council form of government.

What is Camp Dodge and why does it matter to sellers?

Camp Dodge is the headquarters of the Iowa National Guard and sits inside Johnston. Construction began in 1907, and in 1917 the site was turned over to national authorities and greatly expanded as a World War I training center. It is named for Brigadier General Grenville M. Dodge, who organized Iowa's first National Guard unit in 1856.

The post hosts the Sustainment Training Center, the state emergency operations center, the Iowa Law Enforcement Academy and the Iowa Gold Star Military Museum. Johnston also calls itself a Home Base Iowa community, a program that connects veterans with local businesses.

What does Saylorville Lake mean for flood risk near Johnston?

Saylorville Lake is a flood control reservoir on the Des Moines River about 11 miles upstream from Des Moines. Congress authorized it in the Flood Control Act of 1958, excavation began in July 1965 and the dam became fully operational in September 1977 at a cost of $130 million.

The Army Corps of Engineers, Rock Island District, runs the lake. At normal pool it covers about 5,950 acres, and at full flood pool it can reach 16,700 acres. The reservoir hit its record level of 892.03 feet on July 11, 1993.

A house near the river or Beaver Creek should be checked against flood maps before you list. Ask the insurer, ask the city and keep any flood claim records handy.

Its schools are Johnston High School, Johnston Middle School, Summit Middle School, and elementary schools named Beaver Creek, Horizon, Lawson, Timber Ridge and Wallace. A Johnston Early Learning Academy handles preschool.

How do permits, utilities and property tax work in Johnston?

Johnston's City Hall is at 6221 Merle Hay Road, with a phone number of 515-278-2344. The city's website links to permits for accessory buildings, decks and pools, and separate forms cover right-of-way work. Utility start, stop and transfer requests go through the city, and trash and recycling pickup is handled through the MWA collection service.

Property tax comes from Polk County. The first half is due September 1 and the second half March 1, with late interest beginning October 1 and April 1 at 1.5 percent a month. The Polk County Treasurer is at 515-286-3060. Taxes are usually prorated at closing, and the buyer gets a credit or the seller pays the treasurer.

Iowa also applies a transfer tax of eighty cents per $500 of value above the first $500 on deeds with consideration (Iowa Code 428A.1). Assessments are updated every other year, and owners can protest to the Board of Review from April 2 through April 30.

Johnston sits on I-80 and near Iowa Highway 141, which puts downtown Des Moines, Urbandale and the western suburbs within a short drive. DART buses connect the city to the region on routes 5 and 93.

Polk County, which holds Johnston, was created on January 13, 1846, covers about 592 square miles and had 492,401 residents in 2020, making it the most populous county in Iowa. Other Polk County cities in the 2020 ranking include Des Moines, Ankeny, West Des Moines and Urbandale, with Johnston fifth. Polk County sells unpaid taxes at an annual online tax sale, and the buyer receives a lien on the property. In 2024 the sale was held June 17, and an owner could pay by 5:00 p.m. on June 14 to avoid it.

After a tax sale, redemption costs the full delinquent amount plus 2 percent per month, and partial payments are not allowed on a tax sale. If a lien is not redeemed in the time Iowa law sets, the certificate holder can start a tax deed proceeding. A notice to redeem should prompt a call to the treasurer right away.
